segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā vaggumudātīriyānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ cetasā ceto paricca manasi karitvā āyasmantaṁ ānandaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: Then, having applied his mind to comprehending the minds of the mendicants staying on the bank of the Vaggumudā River, the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda,

segs.p: “ālokajātā viya me, ānanda, esā disā, obhāsajātā viya me, ānanda, esā disā;
segs.e: “A light, it appears to me, has arisen in this quarter, Ānanda; a brightness has arisen.

segs.p: yassaṁ disāyaṁ vaggumudātīriyā bhikkhū viharanti gantuṁ appaṭikūlāsi me manasi kātuṁ.
segs.e: I’m not put off at the thought of going to where the mendicants are staying on the bank of the Vaggumudā River.

segs.p: Pahiṇeyyāsi tvaṁ, ānanda, vaggumudātīriyānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ santike dūtaṁ:
segs.e: Send a message to those mendicants:
‘Venerables, the Teacher summons you. He wants to see you.’”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā ānando bhagavato paṭissutvā yena aññataro bhikkhu tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṁ bhikkhuṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” Ānanda replied. He went to one of the mendicants and said,

segs.p: “ehi tvaṁ, āvuso, yena vaggumudātīriyā bhikkhū tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā vaggumudātīriye bhikkhū evaṁ vadehi:
segs.e: “Please, Reverend, go to the mendicants staying on the bank of the Vaggumudā River and say to them,
‘Venerables, the Teacher summons you. He wants to see you.’”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho so bhikkhu āyasmato ānandassa paṭissutvā—
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” replied that mendicant.

segs.p: seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṁ vā bāhaṁ pasāreyya, pasāritaṁ vā bāhaṁ samiñjeyya; evamevaṁ—mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṁ antarahito vaggumudāya nadiyā tīre tesaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ purato pāturahosi.
segs.e: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof, and reappeared in front of those mendicants on the bank of the Vaggumudā River.

segs.p: Atha kho so bhikkhu vaggumudātīriye bhikkhū etadavoca:
segs.e: Then he said to those mendicants,
“Venerables, the Teacher summons you. He wants to see you.”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū tassa bhikkhuno paṭissutvā senāsanaṁ saṁsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya—
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” replied those mendicants. They set their lodgings in order and took their bowls and robes.

segs.p: seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṁ vā bāhaṁ pasāreyya, pasāritaṁ vā bāhaṁ samiñjeyya; evamevaṁ—vaggumudāya nadiyā tīre antarahitā mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṁ bhagavato sammukhe pāturahesuṁ.
segs.e: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, they vanished from the bank of the Vaggumudā River, and reappeared in the presence of the Buddha in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā āneñjena samādhinā nisinno hoti.
segs.e: But at that time the Buddha was sitting immersed in imperturbable meditation.
Then those mendicants thought,

segs.p: “katamena nu kho bhagavā vihārena etarahi viharatī”ti?
segs.e: “What kind of meditation is the Buddha practicing right now?”
They thought,
“He is practicing the imperturbable meditation.”
They all sat in imperturbable meditation.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā ānando abhikkantāya rattiyā, nikkhante paṭhame yāme, uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṁsaṁ uttarāsaṅgaṁ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṁ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: And then, as the night was getting late, in the first watch of the night, Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,

segs.p: “abhikkantā, bhante, ratti; nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo; ciranisinnā āgantukā bhikkhū;
segs.e: “Sir, the night is getting late. It is the first watch of the night, and the visiting mendicants have been sitting long.
Sir, please greet the visiting mendicants.”
But the Buddha kept silent.

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho āyasmā ānando abhikkantāya rattiyā, nikkhante majjhime yāme, uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṁsaṁ uttarāsaṅgaṁ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṁ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a second time, as the night was getting late, in the middle watch of the night, Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,
“Sir, the night is getting late. It is the second watch of the night, and the visiting mendicants have been sitting long.
Sir, please greet the visiting mendicants.”
But for a second time the Buddha kept silent.

segs.p: Tatiyampi kho āyasmā ānando abhikkantāya rattiyā, nikkhante pacchime yāme, uddhaste aruṇe, nandimukhiyā rattiyā uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṁsaṁ uttarāsaṅgaṁ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṁ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a third time, as the night was getting late, in the last watch of the night, as dawn stirred, bringing joy to the night, Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,
“Sir, the night is getting late. It is the last watch of the night; dawn stirs, bringing joy to the night, and the visiting mendicants have been sitting long.
Sir, please greet the visiting mendicants.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvā āyasmantaṁ ānandaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: Then the Buddha emerged from that immersion and addressed Ānanda,

segs.p: “sace kho tvaṁ, ānanda, jāneyyāsi ettakampi te nappaṭibhāseyya.
segs.e: “If you’d known, Ānanda, you wouldn’t have said so much.

segs.p: Ahañca, ānanda, imāni ca pañca bhikkhusatāni sabbeva āneñjasamādhinā nisīdimhā”ti.
segs.e: Both I and these five hundred mendicants have been sitting in imperturbable meditation.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“A mendicant who has beaten <j>the thorn of sensuality—
and abuse, killing, and caging—
steady as a mountain, imperturbable,
trembles not at pleasure and pain.”
Heartfelt Sayings 3.4
With Sāriputta
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā sāriputto bhagavato avidūre nisinno hoti pallaṅkaṁ ābhujitvā ujuṁ kāyaṁ paṇidhāya parimukhaṁ satiṁ upaṭṭhapetvā.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, his body set straight, and mindfulness brought to the present.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ sāriputtaṁ avidūre nisinnaṁ pallaṅkaṁ ābhujitvā ujuṁ kāyaṁ paṇidhāya parimukhaṁ satiṁ upaṭṭhapetvā.
segs.e: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“As a rocky mountain
is unwavering and well grounded,
so when delusion ends,
a monk, like a mountain, doesn’t tremble.”
Heartfelt Sayings 3.5
With Mahāmoggallāna
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavato avidūre nisinno hoti pallaṅkaṁ ābhujitvā ujuṁ kāyaṁ paṇidhāya kāyagatāya satiyā ajjhattaṁ sūpaṭṭhitāya.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight and mindfulness of the body well-established in himself.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ mahāmoggallānaṁ avidūre nisinnaṁ pallaṅkaṁ ābhujitvā ujuṁ kāyaṁ paṇidhāya kāyagatāya satiyā ajjhattaṁ sūpaṭṭhitāya.
segs.e: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“With mindfulness of the body established,
restrained in the six fields of contact,
a mendicant always immersed in samādhi
would know extinguishment in themselves.”
Heartfelt Sayings 3.6
With Pilindavaccha
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā pilindavaccho bhikkhū vasalavādena samudācarati.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Pilindavaccha addressed the mendicants as “lowlifes”.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,
“Sir, Venerable Pilindavaccha addresses the mendicants as ‘lowlifes’.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā aññataraṁ bhikkhuṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

segs.p: “ehi tvaṁ, bhikkhu, mama vacanena pilindavacchaṁ bhikkhuṁ āmantehi:
segs.e: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Pilindavaccha that
the Teacher summons him.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā yenāyasmā pilindavaccho tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ pilindavacchaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Pilindavaccha and said to him,
“Reverend Pilindavaccha, the Teacher summons you.”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā pilindavaccho tassa bhikkhuno paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho āyasmantaṁ pilindavacchaṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” Pilindavaccha replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

segs.p: “saccaṁ kira tvaṁ, vaccha, bhikkhū vasalavādena samudācarasī”ti?
segs.e: “Is it really true, Vaccha, that you addressed the mendicants as ‘lowlifes’?”
“Yes, sir,” he replied.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā āyasmato pilindavacchassa pubbenivāsaṁ manasi karitvā bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: Then, having applied his mind to Pilindavaccha’s past lives, the Buddha said to the mendicants,

segs.p: “mā kho tumhe, bhikkhave, vacchassa bhikkhuno ujjhāyittha.
segs.e: “Mendicants, don’t complain about the mendicant Vaccha.

segs.p: Na, bhikkhave, vaccho dosantaro bhikkhū vasalavādena samudācarati.
segs.e: He doesn’t address the mendicants as ‘lowlifes’ out of hate.

segs.p: Vacchassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno pañca jātisatāni abbokiṇṇāni brāhmaṇakule paccājātāni.
segs.e: For five hundred lives without interruption he was reborn in a brahmin family.
For a long time, he has addressed people as ‘lowlife’.
That’s why he addresses the mendicants as ‘lowlifes’.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“In whom dwells no deceit or conceit,
rid of greed, unselfish, <j>with no need for hope,
with anger cast aside, quenched:

segs.p: So brāhmaṇo so samaṇo sa bhikkhū”ti.
segs.e: they are a brahmin, an ascetic, a mendicant.”
Heartfelt Sayings 3.7
Sakka’s Heartfelt Saying
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahākassapo pippaliguhāyaṁ viharati, sattāhaṁ ekapallaṅkena nisinno hoti aññataraṁ samādhiṁ samāpajjitvā.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pipphali cave. Having entered a certain state of immersion, he sat cross-legged for seven days without moving.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo tassa sattāhassa accayena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhāsi.
segs.e: When seven days had passed, Mahākassapa emerged from that state of immersion.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmato mahākassapassa tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhitassa etadahosi:
segs.e: It occurred to him,
“Why not enter Rājagaha for almsfood?”

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena pañcamattāni devatāsatāni ussukkaṁ āpannāni honti āyasmato mahākassapassa piṇḍapātapaṭilābhāya.
segs.e: Now at that time five hundred deities were ready and eager for the chance to offer alms to Mahākassapa.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo tāni pañcamattāni devatāsatāni paṭikkhipitvā pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṁ piṇḍāya pāvisi.
segs.e: But Mahākasspa turned down those deities. In the morning, he robed up, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena sakko devānamindo āyasmato mahākassapassa piṇḍapātaṁ dātukāmo hoti.
segs.e: Now at that time Sakka, lord of gods, wished to give alms to Mahākassapa.

segs.p: Pesakāravaṇṇaṁ abhinimminitvā tantaṁ vināti. Sujā asurakaññā tasaraṁ pūreti.
segs.e: Having manifested in the appearance of an embroiderer, he wove the thread. The titan maiden Sujā spun it onto the spindle.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo rājagahe sapadānaṁ piṇḍāya caramāno yena sakkassa devānamindassa nivesanaṁ tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: Then, as Mahākassapa wandered indiscriminately for almsfood in Rājagaha, he approached Sakka’s house.

segs.p: Addasā kho sakko devānamindo āyasmantaṁ mahākassapaṁ dūratova āgacchantaṁ.
segs.e: Seeing Mahākassapa coming off in the distance,

segs.p: Disvāna gharā nikkhamitvā paccuggantvā hatthato pattaṁ gahetvā gharaṁ pavisitvā ghaṭiyā odanaṁ uddharitvā pattaṁ pūretvā āyasmato mahākassapassa adāsi.
segs.e: Sakka came out of his house, greeted him, and took the bowl from his hand. He re-entered the house and filled the bowl with rice from the pot.

segs.p: So ahosi piṇḍapāto anekasūpo anekabyañjano anekarasabyañjano.
segs.e: That almsfood had many tasty soups and sauces.
Then it occurred to Mahākassapa,

segs.p: “ko nu kho ayaṁ satto yassāyaṁ evarūpo iddhānubhāvo”ti?
segs.e: “Now, what being is this who has such psychic power?”
It occurred to him,
“This is Sakka, lord of gods.”
Knowing this, he said to Sakka,
“This is your doing, Kosiya;
don’t do such a thing again.”
“But Honorable Kassapa, we too need merit!
We too ought to make merit.”

segs.p: Atha kho sakko devānamindo āyasmantaṁ mahākassapaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā vehāsaṁ abbhuggantvā ākāse antalikkhe tikkhattuṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then Sakka bowed and respectfully circled Mahākassapa, keeping him on his right. Then he rose into the air and, sitting cross-legged in midair, expressed this heartfelt sentiment three times:
“Oh the gift, the best gift is well established in Kassapa!
Oh the gift, the best gift is well established in Kassapa!
Oh the gift, the best gift is well established in Kassapa!”

segs.p: Assosi kho bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya sakkassa devānamindassa vehāsaṁ abbhuggantvā ākāse antalikkhe tikkhattuṁ udānaṁ udānentassa:
segs.e: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha heard Sakka express this heartfelt sentiment while sitting in the sky.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“A mendicant who relies on alms,
self-supported, providing for no other;
the unaffected one is envied by even the gods,
calm and ever mindful.”
Heartfelt Sayings 3.8
One Who Eats Only Almsfood
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena sambahulānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṁ karerimaṇḍalamāḷe sannisinnānaṁ sannipatitānaṁ ayamantarākathā udapādi:
segs.e: Now at that time, after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the pavilion by the kareri tree and this discussion came up among them:

segs.p: “Piṇḍapātiko, āvuso, bhikkhu piṇḍāya caranto labhati kālena kālaṁ manāpike cakkhunā rūpe passituṁ, labhati kālena kālaṁ manāpike sotena sadde sotuṁ, labhati kālena kālaṁ manāpike ghānena gandhe ghāyituṁ, labhati kālena kālaṁ manāpike jivhāya rase sāyituṁ, labhati kālena kālaṁ manāpike kāyena phoṭṭhabbe phusituṁ.
segs.e: “Reverends, when a mendicant who eats only almsfood is wandering for alms, from time to time they get to see pleasing sights, hear pleasing sounds, smell pleasing odors, taste pleasing flavors, and encounter pleasing touches.

segs.p: Piṇḍapātiko, āvuso, bhikkhu sakkato garukato mānito pūjito apacito piṇḍāya carati.
segs.e: They wander for alms being honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed.
Come, we too should eat only almsfood.

segs.p: Mayampi lacchāma kālena kālaṁ manāpike cakkhunā rūpe passituṁ, mayampi lacchāma kālena kālaṁ manāpike sotena sadde sotuṁ, mayampi lacchāma kālena kālaṁ manāpike ghānena gandhe ghāyituṁ, mayampi lacchāma kālena kālaṁ manāpike jivhāya rase sāyituṁ, mayampi lacchāma kālena kālaṁ manāpike kāyena phoṭṭhabbe phusituṁ;
segs.e: From time to time we too will get to see pleasing sights, hear pleasing sounds, smell pleasing odors, taste pleasing flavors, and encounter pleasing touches.

segs.p: mayampi sakkatā garukatā mānitā pūjitā apacitā piṇḍāya carissāmā”ti.
segs.e: We too shall wander for alms being honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed.”

segs.p: Ayañcarahi tesaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ antarākathā hoti vippakatā.
segs.e: At that point the conversation among those mendicants was left unfinished.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena karerimaṇḍalamāḷo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the pavilion by the kareri tree, where he sat down on the seat spread out
and addressed the mendicants:

segs.p: “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā, kā ca pana vo antarākathā vippakatā”ti?
segs.e: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

segs.p: “Idha, bhante, amhākaṁ pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṁ karerimaṇḍalamāḷe sannisinnānaṁ sannipatitānaṁ ayamantarākathā udapādi:
segs.e: So the mendicants told him what they had been talking about. The Buddha said,

segs.p: ‘Piṇḍapātiko, āvuso, bhikkhu piṇḍāya caranto labhati kālena kālaṁ manāpike cakkhunā rūpe passituṁ, labhati kālena kālaṁ manāpike sotena sadde sotuṁ, labhati kālena kālaṁ manāpike ghānena gandhe ghāyituṁ, labhati kālena kālaṁ manāpike jivhāya rase sāyituṁ, labhati kālena kālaṁ manāpike kāyena phoṭṭhabbe phusituṁ.
Piṇḍapātiko, āvuso, bhikkhu sakkato garukato mānito pūjito apacito piṇḍāya carati.
Mayampi lacchāma kālena kālaṁ manāpike cakkhunā rūpe passituṁ …pe…
Mayampi sakkatā garukatā mānitā pūjitā apacitā piṇḍāya carissāmā’ti.
Ayaṁ kho no, bhante, antarākathā vippakatā, atha bhagavā anuppatto”ti.
“Na khvetaṁ, bhikkhave, tumhākaṁ patirūpaṁ kulaputtānaṁ saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajitānaṁ yaṁ tumhe evarūpiṁ kathaṁ katheyyātha.
segs.e: “Mendicants, it is not appropriate for you gentlemen who have gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness to talk about such things.
When you’re sitting together you should do one of two things:

segs.p: dhammī vā kathā ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo”ti.
segs.e: discuss the teachings or keep noble silence.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“A mendicant who relies on alms,
self-supported, providing for no other;
the unaffected one is envied by even the gods,
but not if they’re after popularity and reputation.”
Heartfelt Sayings 3.9
Professions
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena sambahulānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṁ maṇḍalamāḷe sannisinnānaṁ sannipatitānaṁ ayamantarākathā udapādi:
segs.e: Now at that time, after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the pavilion and this discussion came up among them:
“Who knows a craft?
Who is studying which craft?
Which is the best craft?”
In answer, some said that
elephant-craft is the best of crafts.
Others said that the best craft is
horse-craft,
or chariot-craft,
or archery,
or swordsmanship,
or arithmetic,
or accounting,
or calculating,
or writing,
or poetry,
or cosmology,
or geomancy.

segs.p: Ayañcarahi tesaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ antarākathā hoti vippakatā.
segs.e: At that point the conversation among those mendicants was left unfinished.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena maṇḍalamāḷo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the assembly hall. He sat down on the seat spread out,
and addressed the mendicants:

segs.p: “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā, kā ca pana vo antarākathā vippakatā”ti?
segs.e: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

segs.p: “Idha, bhante, amhākaṁ pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṁ maṇḍalamāḷe sannisinnānaṁ ayamantarākathā udapādi:
segs.e: So the mendicants told him what they had been talking about when the Buddha arrived. The Buddha said,

segs.p: Ayaṁ kho no, bhante, antarākathā hoti vippakatā, atha bhagavā anuppatto”ti.
“Na khvetaṁ, bhikkhave, tumhākaṁ patirūpaṁ kulaputtānaṁ saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajitānaṁ yaṁ tumhe evarūpiṁ kathaṁ katheyyātha.
segs.e: “Mendicants, it is not appropriate for you gentlemen who have gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness to talk about such things.
When you’re sitting together you should do one of two things:

segs.p: dhammī vā kathā ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo”ti.
segs.e: discuss the teachings or keep noble silence.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“Living without a craft, light, wanting what is best,
with senses controlled, everywhere free;
a migrant with no bastion, unselfish, <j>with no need for hope,
having given up conceit, wandering alone: <j>that is a mendicant.”
Heartfelt Sayings 3.10
The World
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā uruvelāyaṁ viharati najjā nerañjarāya tīre bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhisambuddho.
segs.e: At one time, when he was first awakened, the Buddha was staying in Uruvelā at the root of the tree of awakening on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sattāhaṁ ekapallaṅkena nisinno hoti vimuttisukhapaṭisaṁvedī.
segs.e: There the Buddha sat cross-legged for seven days without moving, experiencing the bliss of freedom.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā tassa sattāhassa accayena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvā buddhacakkhunā lokaṁ volokesi.
segs.e: When seven days had passed, the Buddha emerged from that state of immersion and surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā buddhacakkhunā volokento satte anekehi santāpehi santappamāne, anekehi ca pariḷāhehi pariḍayhamāne—
segs.e: He saw sentient beings tormented with many torments, and burning with many fevers
born of greed, hate, and delusion.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“This world, born in torment,
overcome by contact, speaks of disease as the self.
For however you imagine it,
it turns out to be something else.
The world is attached to continued existence, <j>overcome by continued existence,
taking pleasure only in continued existence, <j>yet it becomes something else.
What it enjoys, that is the fear;
what it fears, that is the suffering.
But this spiritual life is led
in order to give up continued existence.

segs.p: ‘Ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā bhavena bhavassa vippamokkhamāhaṁsu, sabbe te avippamuttā bhavasmā’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: Of the ascetics and brahmins who say that through continued existence one is freed from continued existence, none are themselves freed from continued existence, I say.

segs.p: ‘Ye vā pana keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā vibhavena bhavassa nissaraṇamāhaṁsu, sabbe te anissaṭā bhavasmā’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: Of the ascetics and brahmins who say that through nonexistence one escapes from existence, none have themselves escaped from existence, I say.

segs.p: Upadhiñhi paṭicca dukkhamidaṁ sambhoti, sabbupādānakkhayā natthi dukkhassa sambhavo.
segs.e: For this suffering originates dependent on all attachment. With the ending of all grasping there is no origination of suffering.
Just look at this world!

segs.p: puthū avijjāya paretā bhūtā bhūtaratā aparimuttā;
segs.e: Mired in many ways by ignorance, beings in love with being are not released from continued existence.

segs.p: ye hi keci bhavā sabbadhi sabbatthatāya sabbe te bhavā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammāti.
segs.e: Whatever states of continued existence there are—everywhere, all over—all are impermanent, suffering, and perishable.
One who sees truly like this,
with right wisdom,
gives up craving for continued existence,
while not looking forward to nonexistence.
Extinguishment comes <j>from the ending of all cravings;
fading away and cessation no residue left behind.
There is no further existence
for that mendicant extinguished by not grasping.
Victorious in battle, such a one has defeated Māra;
they’ve gone beyond all states of existence.”
Heartfelt Sayings 4.1
With Meghiya
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā cālikāyaṁ viharati cālike pabbate.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Cālikā, on the Cālikā mountain.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā meghiyo bhagavato upaṭṭhāko hoti.
segs.e: Now, at that time Venerable Meghiya was the Buddha’s attendant.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā meghiyo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṁ ṭhito kho āyasmā meghiyo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Meghiya went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,
“Sir, I’d like to enter Jantu village for alms.”
“Please, Meghiya, go at your convenience.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā meghiyo pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya jantugāmaṁ piṇḍāya pāvisi.
segs.e: Then Meghiya robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Jantu village for alms.

segs.p: Jantugāme piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena kimikāḷāya nadiyā tīraṁ tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: After the meal, on his return from almsround in Jantu village, he went to the shore of Kimikālā River.

segs.p: Addasā kho āyasmā meghiyo kimikāḷāya nadiyā tīre jaṅghāvihāraṁ anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno ambavanaṁ pāsādikaṁ manuññaṁ ramaṇīyaṁ.
segs.e: As he was going for a walk along the shore of the river he saw a lovely and delightful mango grove.
Seeing this, it occurred to him,

segs.p: “pāsādikaṁ vatidaṁ ambavanaṁ manuññaṁ ramaṇīyaṁ. Alaṁ vatidaṁ kulaputtassa padhānatthikassa padhānāya.
segs.e: “Oh, this mango grove is lovely and delightful! This is good enough for striving for a gentleman wanting to strive.

segs.p: Sace maṁ bhagavā anujāneyya, āgaccheyyāhaṁ imaṁ ambavanaṁ padhānāyā”ti.
segs.e: If the Buddha allows me, I’ll come back to this mango grove to meditate.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā meghiyo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: Then Venerable Meghiya went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened, adding,

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā meghiyo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
“Idhāhaṁ, bhante, pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya jantugāmaṁ piṇḍāya pāvisiṁ.
Jantugāme piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena kimikāḷāya nadiyā tīraṁ tenupasaṅkamiṁ.
Addasaṁ kho ahaṁ, bhante, kimikāḷāya nadiyā tīre jaṅghāvihāraṁ anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno ambavanaṁ pāsādikaṁ manuññaṁ ramaṇīyaṁ.
Sace maṁ bhagavā anujāneyya, āgaccheyyāhaṁ imaṁ ambavanaṁ padhānāyā’ti.
Sace maṁ, bhante, bhagavā anujānāti, gaccheyyāhaṁ taṁ ambavanaṁ padhānāyā”ti.
segs.e: “If the Buddha allows me, I’ll go back to that mango grove to meditate.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, bhagavā āyasmantaṁ meghiyaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When he had spoken, the Buddha said to him,

segs.p: “āgamehi tāva, meghiya, ekakamhi tāva, yāva aññopi koci bhikkhu āgacchatī”ti.
segs.e: “We’re alone, Meghiya. Wait until another mendicant comes.”

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho āyasmā meghiyo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a second time Meghiya said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “bhagavato, bhante, natthi kiñci uttari karaṇīyaṁ, natthi katassa vā paticayo.
segs.e: “Sir, the Buddha has nothing more to do, and nothing that needs improvement.

segs.p: Mayhaṁ kho pana, bhante, atthi uttari karaṇīyaṁ, atthi katassa paticayo.
segs.e: But I have.

segs.p: Sace maṁ bhagavā anujānāti, gaccheyyāhaṁ taṁ ambavanaṁ padhānāyā”ti.
segs.e: If you allow me, I’ll go back to that mango grove to meditate.”

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ meghiyaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a second time the Buddha said,

segs.p: “āgamehi tāva, meghiya, ekakamhi tāva, yāva aññopi koci bhikkhu āgacchatī”ti.
segs.e: “We’re alone, Meghiya. Wait until another mendicant comes.”

segs.p: Tatiyampi kho āyasmā meghiyo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a third time Meghiya said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “bhagavato, bhante, natthi kiñci uttari karaṇīyaṁ, natthi katassa vā paticayo.
segs.e: “Sir, the Buddha has nothing more to do, and nothing that needs improvement.

segs.p: Mayhaṁ kho pana, bhante, atthi uttari karaṇīyaṁ, atthi katassa paticayo.
segs.e: But I have.

segs.p: Sace maṁ bhagavā anujānāti, gaccheyyāhaṁ taṁ ambavanaṁ padhānāyā”ti.
segs.e: If you allow me, I’ll go back to that mango grove to meditate.”
“Meghiya, since you speak of striving in meditation, what can I say?
Please, Meghiya, go at your convenience.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā meghiyo uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā yena taṁ ambavanaṁ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṁ ambavanaṁ ajjhogāhetvā aññatarasmiṁ rukkhamūle divāvihāraṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: Then Meghiya got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right. Then he went to that mango grove, and, having plunged deep into it, sat at the root of a certain tree for the day’s meditation.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmato meghiyassa tasmiṁ ambavane viharantassa yebhuyyena tayo pāpakā akusalā vitakkā samudācaranti, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: But while Meghiya was meditating in that mango grove he was beset mostly by three kinds of bad, unskillful thoughts, namely,
sensual, malicious, and cruel thoughts.
Then he thought,
“Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing!

segs.p: Saddhāya ca vatamhā agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajitā.
segs.e: I’ve gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness,

segs.p: Atha ca panimehi tīhi pāpakehi akusalehi vitakkehi anvāsattā, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: but I’m still harassed by these three kinds of bad, unskillful thoughts:
sensual, malicious, and cruel thoughts.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā meghiyo sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā meghiyo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Meghiya came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and told the Buddha what had happened.

segs.p: “idha mayhaṁ, bhante, tasmiṁ ambavane viharantassa yebhuyyena tayo pāpakā akusalā vitakkā samudācaranti, seyyathidaṁ—
Saddhāya ca vatamhā agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajitā.
Atha ca panimehi tīhi pāpakehi akusalehi vitakkehi anvāsattā, seyyathidaṁ—
“Aparipakkāya, meghiya, cetovimuttiyā pañca dhammā paripākāya saṁvattanti.
segs.e: “Meghiya, when the heart’s release is not ripe, five things help it ripen.
What five?

segs.p: Idha, meghiya, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto hoti kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko.
segs.e: Firstly, a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates.

segs.p: Aparipakkāya, meghiya, cetovimuttiyā ayaṁ paṭhamo dhammo paripākāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: This is the first thing …

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, meghiya, bhikkhu sīlavā hoti, pātimokkhasaṁvarasaṁvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno, aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī, samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu.
segs.e: Furthermore, a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

segs.p: Aparipakkāya, meghiya, cetovimuttiyā ayaṁ dutiyo dhammo paripākāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: This is the second thing …

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, meghiya, bhikkhu yāyaṁ kathā abhisallekhikā cetovivaraṇasappāyā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṁvattati, seyyathidaṁ—appicchakathā, santuṭṭhikathā, pavivekakathā, asaṁsaggakathā, vīriyārambhakathā, sīlakathā, samādhikathā, paññākathā, vimuttikathā, vimuttiñāṇadassanakathā; evarūpāya kathāya nikāmalābhī hoti akicchalābhī akasiralābhī.
segs.e: Furthermore, a mendicant gets to take part in talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart and leads solely to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment when they want, without trouble or difficulty. That is, talk about fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, aloofness, arousing energy, ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom.

segs.p: Aparipākāya, meghiya, cetovimuttiyā ayaṁ tatiyo dhammo paripākāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: This is the third thing …

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, meghiya, bhikkhu āraddhavīriyo viharati, akusalānaṁ dhammānaṁ pahānāya, kusalānaṁ dhammānaṁ upasampadāya, thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu.
segs.e: Furthermore, a mendicant lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

segs.p: Aparipakkāya, meghiya, cetovimuttiyā ayaṁ catuttho dhammo paripākāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: This is the fourth thing …

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, meghiya, bhikkhu paññavā hoti udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā.
segs.e: Furthermore, a mendicant is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

segs.p: Aparipakkāya, meghiya, cetovimuttiyā ayaṁ pañcamo dhammo paripākāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: This is the fifth thing that, when the heart’s release is not ripe, helps it ripen.

segs.p: Aparipakkāya, meghiya, cetovimuttiyā ime pañca dhammā paripākāya saṁvattanti.
segs.e: These are the five things that, when the heart’s release is not ripe, help it ripen.

segs.p: Kalyāṇamittassetaṁ, meghiya, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṁ kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa yaṁ sīlavā bhavissati, pātimokkhasaṁvarasaṁvuto viharissati, ācāragocarasampanno, aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī, samādāya sikkhissati sikkhāpadesu.
segs.e: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to be ethical …

segs.p: Kalyāṇamittassetaṁ, meghiya, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṁ kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa yaṁ yāyaṁ kathā abhisallekhikā cetovivaraṇasappāyā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṁvattati, seyyathidaṁ—appicchakathā, santuṭṭhikathā, pavivekakathā, asaṁsaggakathā, vīriyārambhakathā, sīlakathā, samādhikathā, paññākathā, vimuttikathā, vimuttiñāṇadassanakathā; evarūpāya kathāya nikāmalābhī bhavissati akicchalābhī akasiralābhī.
segs.e: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to take part in talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart …

segs.p: Kalyāṇamittassetaṁ, meghiya, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṁ kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa yaṁ āraddhavīriyo viharissati akusalānaṁ dhammānaṁ pahānāya, kusalānaṁ dhammānaṁ upasampadāya, thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu.
segs.e: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to be energetic …

segs.p: Kalyāṇamittassetaṁ, meghiya, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṁ kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa yaṁ paññavā bhavissati, udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā.
segs.e: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to be wise …

segs.p: Tena ca pana, meghiya, bhikkhunā imesu pañcasu dhammesu patiṭṭhāya cattāro dhammā uttari bhāvetabbā—
segs.e: But then, a mendicant grounded on these five things should develop four further things.

segs.p: asubhā bhāvetabbā rāgassa pahānāya, mettā bhāvetabbā byāpādassa pahānāya, ānāpānassati bhāvetabbā vitakkupacchedāya, aniccasaññā bhāvetabbā asmimānasamugghātāya.
segs.e: They should develop the perception of ugliness to give up greed, love to give up hate, mindfulness of breathing to cut off thinking, and perception of impermanence to uproot the conceit ‘I am’.
When you perceive impermanence, the perception of not-self becomes stabilized.

segs.p: anattasaññī asmimānasamugghātaṁ pāpuṇāti diṭṭheva dhamme nibbānan”ti.
segs.e: Perceiving not-self, you uproot the conceit ‘I am’ and attain extinguishment in this very life.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“Lesser thoughts and subtle thoughts
arise, springing up in the mind.
Not understanding these thoughts,
one with mind astray runs from one thing to the next.
Having understood these thoughts
that arise, springing up in the mind,
an awakened one—keen, restrained, and mindful—
has given them up without remainder.”
Heartfelt Sayings 4.2
Restless
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā kusinārāyaṁ viharati upavattane mallānaṁ sālavane.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying in the sal forest of the Mallas at Upavattana near Kusinārā.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū bhagavato avidūre araññakuṭikāyaṁ viharanti uddhatā unnaḷā capalā mukharā vikiṇṇavācā muṭṭhassatino asampajānā asamāhitā vibbhantacittā pākatindriyā.
segs.e: Now at that time several mendicants were staying not far from the Buddha in a wilderness hut. They were haughty, insolent, fickle, scurrilous, loose-tongued, unmindful, lacking situational awareness and immersion, with straying minds and undisciplined faculties.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā te sambahule bhikkhū avidūre araññakuṭikāyaṁ viharante uddhate unnaḷe capale mukhare vikiṇṇavāce muṭṭhassatino asampajāne asamāhite vibbhantacitte pākatindriye.
segs.e: The Buddha saw those mendicants staying nearby.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“Unguarded in body,
ruined by wrong view,
overcome with dullness and drowsiness,
you fall under Māra’s sway.
That’s why you should guard the mind,
with right thoughts your habitat,
and right view at the fore.
Having understood rise and fall,
a mendicant who has overcome <j>dullness and drowsiness
would abandon all bad destinies.”
Heartfelt Sayings 4.3
The Cowherd
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā kosalesu cārikaṁ carati mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṁ.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā maggā okkamma yena aññataraṁ rukkhamūlaṁ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: And then the Buddha left the road, went to the root of a certain tree, and sat down on the seat spread out.

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro gopālako yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: Then a certain cowherd went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho taṁ gopālakaṁ bhagavā dhammiyā kathāya sandassesi samādapesi samuttejesi sampahaṁsesi.
segs.e: The Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired him with a Dhamma talk.

segs.p: Atha kho so gopālako bhagavatā dhammiyā kathāya sandassito samādapito samuttejito sampahaṁsito bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the cowherd said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “adhivāsetu me, bhante, bhagavā svātanāya bhattaṁ saddhiṁ bhikkhusaṅghenā”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, would the Buddha, together with the mendicant Saṅgha, please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?”
The Buddha consented with silence.

segs.p: Atha kho so gopālako bhagavato adhivāsanaṁ viditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā pakkāmi.
segs.e: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, the cowherd rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

segs.p: Atha kho so gopālako tassā rattiyā accayena sake nivesane pahūtaṁ appodakapāyāsaṁ paṭiyādāpetvā navañca sappiṁ bhagavato kālaṁ ārocesi:
segs.e: And when the night had passed the cowherd had plenty of thick milk-rice prepared in his own home, with fresh ghee. Then he had the Buddha informed of the time, saying,
“Sir, it’s time. The meal is ready.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya saddhiṁ bhikkhusaṅghena yena tassa gopālakassa nivesanaṁ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: The Buddha robed up, took his bowl and robe and, together with the Saṅgha of monks, went to the house of that cowherd, where he sat down on the prepared seat in the dining hall.

segs.p: Atha kho so gopālako buddhappamukhaṁ bhikkhusaṅghaṁ appodakapāyāsena navena ca sappinā sahatthā santappesi sampavāresi.
segs.e: Then the cowherd served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with his own hands with a thick milk-rice and fresh ghee.

segs.p: Atha kho so gopālako bhagavantaṁ bhuttāviṁ onītapattapāṇiṁ aññataraṁ nīcaṁ āsanaṁ gahetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, the cowherd took a low seat and sat to one side.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho taṁ gopālakaṁ bhagavā dhammiyā kathāya sandassetvā samādapetvā samuttejetvā sampahaṁsetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi.
segs.e: The Buddha then educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired him with a teaching, after which he got up and left.

segs.p: Atha kho acirapakkantassa bhagavato taṁ gopālakaṁ aññataro puriso sīmantarikāya jīvitā voropesi.
segs.e: But soon after the Buddha had left, the cowherd was killed by a certain man in the gap between village perimeters.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

segs.p: “yena, bhante, gopālakena ajja buddhappamukho bhikkhusaṅgho appodakapāyāsena navena ca sappinā sahatthā santappito sampavārito so kira, bhante, gopālako aññatarena purisena sīmantarikāya jīvitā voropito”ti.
Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“A wrongly directed mind
would do you more harm
than a hater to the hated,
or an enemy to their foe.”
Heartfelt Sayings 4.4
The Spirit’s Blow
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca mahāmoggallāno kapotakandarāyaṁ viharanti.
segs.e: At that time the venerables Sāriputta and Moggallāna were staying near the pigeons’ alcove.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā sāriputto juṇhāya rattiyā navoropitehi kesehi abbhokāse nisinno hoti aññataraṁ samādhiṁ samāpajjitvā.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting outdoors in the moonlight, his head freshly shaven, having entered a certain state of immersion.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena dve yakkhā sahāyakā uttarāya disāya dakkhiṇaṁ disaṁ gacchanti kenacideva karaṇīyena.
segs.e: Now at that time two native spirits who were friends were on their way from the north to the south on some business.

segs.p: Addasaṁsu kho te yakkhā āyasmantaṁ sāriputtaṁ juṇhāya rattiyā navoropitehi kesehi abbhokāse nisinnaṁ.
segs.e: They saw Sāriputta meditating there.

segs.p: Disvāna eko yakkho dutiyaṁ yakkhaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: One of the spirits said to the other,

segs.p: “paṭibhāti maṁ, samma, imassa samaṇassa sīse pahāraṁ dātun”ti.
segs.e: “I feel inspired, my dear, to give this ascetic a blow on the head!”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, so yakkho taṁ yakkhaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: The other spirit replied,
“Enough, my dear, don’t hit the ascetic!

segs.p: Uḷāro so, samma, samaṇo mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo”ti.
segs.e: That is an eminent ascetic, powerful and mighty!”

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho so yakkho taṁ yakkhaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a second time the first spirit said to the other,

segs.p: “paṭibhāti maṁ, samma, imassa samaṇassa sīse pahāraṁ dātun”ti.
segs.e: “I feel inspired to give this ascetic a blow on the head!”

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho so yakkho taṁ yakkhaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a second time, the other spirit replied,
“Enough, don’t hit the ascetic!

segs.p: Uḷāro so, samma, samaṇo mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo”ti.
segs.e: That is an eminent ascetic, powerful and mighty!”

segs.p: Tatiyampi kho so yakkho taṁ yakkhaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a third time the first spirit said to the other,

segs.p: “paṭibhāti maṁ, samma, imassa samaṇassa sīse pahāraṁ dātun”ti.
segs.e: “I feel inspired to give this ascetic a blow on the head!”

segs.p: Tatiyampi kho so yakkho taṁ yakkhaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a third time, the other spirit replied,
“Enough, don’t hit the ascetic!

segs.p: Uḷāro so, samma, samaṇo mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo”ti.
segs.e: That is an eminent ascetic, powerful and mighty!”

segs.p: Atha kho so yakkho taṁ yakkhaṁ anādiyitvā āyasmato sāriputtattherassa sīse pahāraṁ adāsi.
segs.e: Ignoring his friend, the first spirit struck Sāriputta.

segs.p: Tāva mahā pahāro ahosi, api tena pahārena sattaratanaṁ vā aḍḍhaṭṭhamaratanaṁ vā nāgaṁ osādeyya, mahantaṁ vā pabbatakūṭaṁ padāleyya.
segs.e: The blow was so strong it would have felled a bull elephant seven or seven and a half cubits tall, or split apart a great mountain peak.

segs.p: Atha ca pana so yakkho “ḍayhāmi ḍayhāmī”ti vatvā tattheva mahānirayaṁ apatāsi.
segs.e: But then the spirit, crying out, “I burn, I burn!” fell into the Great Hell right there.

segs.p: Addasā kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena tena yakkhena āyasmato sāriputtattherassa sīse pahāraṁ dīyamānaṁ.
segs.e: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, Venerable Moggallāna saw that spirit striking Venerable Sāriputta.

segs.p: Disvā yena āyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ sāriputtaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: He approached him and said,

segs.p: “kacci te, āvuso, khamanīyaṁ, kacci yāpanīyaṁ, kacci na kiñci dukkhan”ti?
segs.e: “I hope you’re keeping well, reverend, I hope you’re all right. I hope you are not in pain.”

segs.p: “Khamanīyaṁ me, āvuso moggallāna, yāpanīyaṁ me, āvuso moggallāna;
segs.e: “I am keeping well, Reverend Moggallāna;

segs.p: api ca me sīsaṁ thokaṁ dukkhan”ti.
segs.e: but my head does hurt a little.”
“It’s incredible, Reverend Sāriputta, it’s amazing!
How mighty and powerful is Venerable Sāriputta!

segs.p: Idha te, āvuso sāriputta, aññataro yakkho sīse pahāraṁ adāsi.
segs.e: Just now, a native spirit struck you on the head.

segs.p: Tāva mahā pahāro ahosi, api tena pahārena sattaratanaṁ vā aḍḍhaṭṭhamaratanaṁ vā nāgaṁ osādeyya, mahantaṁ vā pabbatakūṭaṁ padāleyya, atha ca panāyasmā sāriputto evamāha:
segs.e: The blow was so strong it would have felled a bull elephant seven or seven and a half cubits tall, or split apart a great mountain peak.

segs.p: ‘khamanīyaṁ me, āvuso moggallāna, yāpanīyaṁ me, āvuso moggallāna;
segs.e: Yet you say, ‘I am keeping well, Reverend Moggallāna;

segs.p: api ca me sīsaṁ thokaṁ dukkhan’”ti.
segs.e: but my head does hurt a little.’”
“It’s incredible, Reverend Moggallāna, it’s amazing!

segs.p: Yāva mahiddhiko āyasmā mahāmoggallāno mahānubhāvo yatra hi nāma yakkhampi passissati.
segs.e: How mighty and powerful is Venerable Moggallāna, in that he can even see a native spirit!
Whereas I can’t even see a mud-goblin right now.”

segs.p: Assosi kho bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya tesaṁ ubhinnaṁ mahānāgānaṁ imaṁ evarūpaṁ kathāsallāpaṁ.
segs.e: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha heard that discussion between those two spiritual giants.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“One whose mind is like a rock,
steady, never shaking,
free of desire for desirable things,
not getting annoyed when things are annoying:
from where will suffering strike one
whose mind is developed like this?”
Heartfelt Sayings 4.5
A Bull Elephant
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā kosambiyaṁ viharati ghositārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā ākiṇṇo viharati bhikkhūhi bhikkhunīhi upāsakehi upāsikāhi rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi.
segs.e: Now at that time Buddha lived crowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and monastics of other religions and their disciples.
Crowded, he lived in suffering and discomfort.
Then he thought,

segs.p: “ahaṁ kho etarahi ākiṇṇo viharāmi bhikkhūhi bhikkhunīhi upāsakehi upāsikāhi rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi.
segs.e: “These days I live crowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and monastics of other religions and their disciples.
Crowded, I live in suffering and discomfort.
Why don’t I live alone, withdrawn from the group?”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya kosambiṁ piṇḍāya pāvisi.
segs.e: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms.

segs.p: Kosambiyaṁ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto sāmaṁ senāsanaṁ saṁsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anāmantetvā upaṭṭhākaṁ anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṁ eko adutiyo yena pālileyyakaṁ tena cārikaṁ pakkāmi.
segs.e: After the meal, on his return from almsround, he set his lodgings in order himself. Taking his bowl and robe, without informing his supporters or taking leave of the mendicant Saṅgha, he set out to go wandering alone toward Pārileyyaka, with no companion.

segs.p: Anupubbena cārikaṁ caramāno yena pālileyyakaṁ tadavasari.
segs.e: When he eventually arrived,

segs.p: Tatra sudaṁ bhagavā pālileyyake viharati rakkhitavanasaṇḍe bhaddasālamūle.
segs.e: he stayed in a protected forest grove, at the foot of a sacred sal tree.

segs.p: Aññataropi kho hatthināgo ākiṇṇo viharati hatthīhi hatthinīhi hatthikalabhehi hatthicchāpehi. Chinnaggāni ceva tiṇāni khādati, obhaggobhaggañcassa sākhābhaṅgaṁ khādanti, āvilāni ca pānīyāni pivati, ogāhā cassa uttiṇṇassa hatthiniyo kāyaṁ upanighaṁsantiyo gacchanti.
segs.e: A certain bull elephant was also living crowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs. He ate the grass they’d trampled, and they ate the broken branches he dragged down. He drank muddy water, and after his bath the female elephants bumped into him.
Crowded, he lived in suffering and discomfort.
Then he thought,

segs.p: “ahaṁ kho etarahi ākiṇṇo viharāmi hatthīhi hatthinīhi hatthikalabhehi hatthicchāpehi, chinnaggāni ceva tiṇāni khādāmi, obhaggobhaggañca me sākhābhaṅgaṁ khādanti, āvilāni ca pānīyāni pivāmi, ogāhā ca me uttiṇṇassa hatthiniyo kāyaṁ upanighaṁsantiyo gacchanti, ākiṇṇo dukkhaṁ na phāsu viharāmi.
segs.e: “These days I live crowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs. I eat the grass they’ve trampled, and they eat the broken branches I’ve dragged down. I drink muddy water, and after my bath the female elephants bump into me. Crowded, I live in suffering and discomfort.
Why don’t I live alone, withdrawn from the herd?”

segs.p: Atha kho so hatthināgo yūthā apakkamma yena pālileyyakaṁ rakkhitavanasaṇḍo bhaddasālamūlaṁ yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: So he left the herd and went to Pārileyyaka, where he approached the Buddha in the protected forest grove at the foot of a sacred sal tree.

segs.p: Tatra sudaṁ so hatthināgo yasmiṁ padese bhagavā viharati taṁ padesaṁ appaharitaṁ karoti, soṇḍāya ca bhagavato pānīyaṁ paribhojanīyaṁ upaṭṭhāpeti.
segs.e: There he attended on the Buddha, clearing the vegetation from the place where the Buddha stayed, and using his trunk to set out water for drinking and washing.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavato rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: Then as the Buddha was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

segs.p: “ahaṁ kho pubbe ākiṇṇo vihāsiṁ bhikkhūhi bhikkhunīhi upāsakehi upāsikāhi rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi, ākiṇṇo dukkhaṁ na phāsu vihāsiṁ.
segs.e: “Formerly I lived crowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and monastics of other religions and their disciples. Crowded, I live in suffering and discomfort.

segs.p: Somhi etarahi anākiṇṇo viharāmi bhikkhūhi bhikkhunīhi upāsakehi upāsikāhi rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi, anākiṇṇo sukhaṁ phāsu viharāmī”ti.
segs.e: But now I live uncrowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and monastics of other religions and their disciples. Being uncrowded, I live in happiness and comfort.”

segs.p: Tassapi kho hatthināgassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: And to the bull elephant also this thought came to mind,

segs.p: “ahaṁ kho pubbe ākiṇṇo vihāsiṁ hatthīhi hatthinīhi hatthikalabhehi hatthicchāpehi, chinnaggāni ceva tiṇāni khādiṁ, obhaggobhaggañca me sākhābhaṅgaṁ khādiṁsu, āvilāni ca pānīyāni apāyiṁ, ogāhā ca me uttiṇṇassa hatthiniyo kāyaṁ upanighaṁsantiyo agamaṁsu, ākiṇṇo dukkhaṁ na phāsu vihāsiṁ.
segs.e: “Formerly I lived crowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs. I ate the grass they’d trampled, and they ate the broken branches I’d dragged down. I drank muddy water, and after my bath the female elephants bumped into me. Crowded, I lived in suffering and discomfort.

segs.p: Somhi etarahi anākiṇṇo viharāmi hatthīhi hatthinīhi hatthikalabhehi hatthicchāpehi, acchinnaggāni ceva tiṇāni khādāmi, obhaggobhaggañca me sākhābhaṅgaṁ na khādanti, anāvilāni ca pānīyāni pivāmi, ogāhā ca me uttiṇṇassa hatthiniyo na kāyaṁ upanighaṁsantiyo gacchanti, anākiṇṇo sukhaṁ phāsu viharāmī”ti.
segs.e: But now I live uncrowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs. I eat untrampled grass, and other elephants don’t eat the broken branches I have dragged down. I don’t drink muddy water, and the female elephants don’t bump into me after my bath. Being uncrowded, I live in happiness and comfort.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā attano ca pavivekaṁ viditvā tassa ca hatthināgassa cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding his own seclusion and knowing that elephant’s train of thought, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“The giant elephant,
with tusks like draft-poles,
agrees heart to heart with the spiritual giant,
since each finds joy in the woods alone.”
Heartfelt Sayings 4.6
The Alms-Gatherer
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā piṇḍolabhāradvājo bhagavato avidūre nisinno hoti pallaṅkaṁ ābhujitvā ujuṁ kāyaṁ paṇidhāya āraññiko piṇḍapātiko paṁsukūliko tecīvariko appiccho santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṁsaṭṭho āraddhavīriyo dhutavādo adhicittamanuyutto.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight. He was one who lived in the wilderness, ate only almsfood, wore rag robes, and owned just three robes. He was of few wishes, content, secluded, aloof, and energetic, an advocate of austerities, dedicated to the higher mind.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ piṇḍolabhāradvājaṁ avidūre nisinnaṁ pallaṅkaṁ ābhujitvā ujuṁ kāyaṁ paṇidhāya āraññikaṁ piṇḍapātikaṁ paṁsukūlikaṁ tecīvarikaṁ appicchaṁ santuṭṭhaṁ pavivittaṁ asaṁsaṭṭhaṁ āraddhavīriyaṁ dhutavādaṁ adhicittamanuyuttaṁ.
segs.e: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“Not speaking ill nor doing harm;
restraint in the monastic code;
moderation in eating;
staying in remote lodgings;
commitment to the higher mind—
this is the instruction of the Buddhas.”
Heartfelt Sayings 4.7
With Sāriputta
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā sāriputto bhagavato avidūre nisinno hoti pallaṅkaṁ ābhujitvā ujuṁ kāyaṁ paṇidhāya appiccho santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṁsaṭṭho āraddhavīriyo adhicittamanuyutto.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight. He was of few wishes, content, secluded, aloof, energetic, dedicated to the higher mind.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ sāriputtaṁ avidūre nisinnaṁ pallaṅkaṁ ābhujitvā ujuṁ kāyaṁ paṇidhāya appicchaṁ santuṭṭhaṁ pavivittaṁ asaṁsaṭṭhaṁ āraddhavīriyaṁ adhicittamanuyuttaṁ.
segs.e: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“A sage of higher consciousness, diligent,
training in the ways of sagacity:
there are no sorrows for the unaffected,
calm and ever mindful.”
Heartfelt Sayings 4.8
With Sundarī
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṁ.
segs.e: Now at that time the Buddha was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And he received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

segs.p: Bhikkhusaṅghopi sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṁ.
segs.e: And the mendicant Saṅgha was also honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And they received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

segs.p: Aññatitthiyā pana paribbājakā asakkatā honti agarukatā amānitā apūjitā anapacitā na lābhino cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṁ.
segs.e: But the wanderers who followed other religions were not honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And they didn’t receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

segs.p: Atha kho te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā bhagavato sakkāraṁ asahamānā bhikkhusaṅghassa ca yena sundarī paribbājikā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā sundariṁ paribbājikaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then those wanderers who followed other religions, unable to bear the esteem of the mendicant Saṅgha, approached the female wanderer Sundarī and said,
“Sister, are you able to do something for the welfare of your kin?”
“What can I do, masters?
How can I help?
I’d even give my life for the welfare of my kin.”
“Well then, sister, frequently visit Jeta’s Grove.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, ayyā”ti kho sundarī paribbājikā tesaṁ aññatitthiyānaṁ paribbājakānaṁ paṭissutvā abhikkhaṇaṁ jetavanaṁ agamāsi.
segs.e: “Yes, masters,” she replied, and did as they asked.
When those wanderers knew

segs.p: “vodiṭṭhā kho sundarī paribbājikā bahujanena abhikkhaṇaṁ jetavanaṁ gacchantī”ti.
segs.e: that Sundarī had been clearly seen by many people frequently visiting Jeta’s Grove,

segs.p: Atha naṁ jīvitā voropetvā tattheva jetavanassa parikhākūpe nikkhipitvā yena rājā pasenadi kosalo tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: they killed her and dumped her in the ditch around Jeta’s Grove. Then they went to see King Pasenadi of Kosala and said to him,

segs.p: “yā sā, mahārāja, sundarī paribbājikā; sā no na dissatī”ti.
segs.e: “Great king, we cannot find the female wanderer Sundarī.”
“But where do you suspect she is?”
“At Jeta’s Grove, Great King.”
“Well then, search Jeta’s Grove.”

segs.p: Atha kho te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā jetavanaṁ vicinitvā yathānikkhittaṁ parikhākūpā uddharitvā mañcakaṁ āropetvā sāvatthiṁ pavesetvā rathiyāya rathiyaṁ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṁ upasaṅkamitvā manusse ujjhāpesuṁ:
segs.e: So the wanderers searched Jeta’s Grove. They pulled her body up from the ditch where they had dumped it, and lifted it on a bier. Having entered Sāvatthī, they went from street to street and from square to square, complaining to people:
“See the deed of the ascetics who follow the Sakyan!

segs.p: Alajjino ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā dussīlā pāpadhammā musāvādino abrahmacārino.
segs.e: Shameless are these ascetics who follow the Sakyan, immoral and wicked. They are liars and unchaste.

segs.p: Ime hi nāma dhammacārino samacārino brahmacārino saccavādino sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā paṭijānissanti.
segs.e: Sure, they claim to be of principled and moral conduct, to be chaste, truthful, ethical, and of good character.

segs.p: Natthi imesaṁ sāmaññaṁ, natthi imesaṁ brahmaññaṁ.
segs.e: But they have no asceticism, no spirituality.

segs.p: Naṭṭhaṁ imesaṁ sāmaññaṁ, naṭṭhaṁ imesaṁ brahmaññaṁ.
segs.e: Asceticism and spirituality are lost to them!

segs.p: Kuto imesaṁ sāmaññaṁ, kuto imesaṁ brahmaññaṁ?
segs.e: Where is their asceticism, where their spirituality?

segs.p: Apagatā ime sāmaññā, apagatā ime brahmaññā.
segs.e: They have abandoned asceticism and spirituality!

segs.p: Kathañhi nāma puriso purisakiccaṁ karitvā itthiṁ jīvitā voropessatī”ti.
segs.e: How on earth can a man, having done a man’s business, kill a woman!”

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena sāvatthiyaṁ manussā bhikkhū disvā asabbhāhi pharusāhi vācāhi akkosanti paribhāsanti rosanti vihesanti:
segs.e: Then at that time when the people of Sāvatthī saw the mendicants they abused and insulted them with rude, harsh words:

segs.p: “Alajjino ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā dussīlā pāpadhammā musāvādino abrahmacārino.
segs.e: “Shameless are these ascetics who follow the Sakyan, immoral, wicked. They are liars and unchaste.

segs.p: Ime hi nāma dhammacārino samacārino brahmacārino saccavādino sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā paṭijānissanti.
segs.e: Sure, they claim to be of principled and moral conduct, to be chaste, truthful, ethical, and of good character.

segs.p: Natthi imesaṁ sāmaññaṁ, natthi imesaṁ brahmaññaṁ.
segs.e: But they have no asceticism, no spirituality.

segs.p: Naṭṭhaṁ imesaṁ sāmaññaṁ, naṭṭhaṁ imesaṁ brahmaññaṁ.
segs.e: Asceticism and spirituality are lost to them!

segs.p: Kuto imesaṁ sāmaññaṁ, kuto imesaṁ brahmaññaṁ?
segs.e: Where is their asceticism, where their spirituality?

segs.p: Apagatā ime sāmaññā, apagatā ime brahmaññā.
segs.e: They have abandoned asceticism and spirituality!

segs.p: Kathañhi nāma puriso purisakiccaṁ karitvā itthiṁ jīvitā voropessatī”ti.
segs.e: How on earth can a man, having done a man’s business, kill a woman!”

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṁ piṇḍāya pāvisiṁsu.
segs.e: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

segs.p: Sāvatthiyaṁ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

segs.p: “Etarahi, bhante, sāvatthiyaṁ manussā bhikkhū disvā asabbhāhi pharusāhi vācāhi akkosanti paribhāsanti rosanti vihesanti:
‘alajjino ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā dussīlā pāpadhammā musāvādino abrahmacārino.
Ime hi nāma dhammacārino samacārino brahmacārino saccavādino sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā paṭijānissanti.
Natthi imesaṁ sāmaññaṁ, natthi imesaṁ brahmaññaṁ.
Naṭṭhaṁ imesaṁ sāmaññaṁ, naṭṭhaṁ imesaṁ brahmaññaṁ.
Kuto imesaṁ sāmaññaṁ, kuto imesaṁ brahmaññaṁ?
Apagatā ime sāmaññā, apagatā ime brahmaññā.
Kathañhi nāma puriso purisakiccaṁ karitvā itthiṁ jīvitā voropessatī’”ti.
“Neso, bhikkhave, saddo ciraṁ bhavissati sattāhameva bhavissati. Sattāhassa accayena antaradhāyissati.
segs.e: “That rumor, mendicants, won’t last long. It will only be seven days, then it will vanish.
segs.s: several mendicants robed up in the morning and

segs.p: Tena hi, bhikkhave, ye manussā bhikkhū disvā asabbhāhi pharusāhi vācāhi akkosanti paribhāsanti rosanti vihesanti, te tumhe imāya gāthāya paṭicodetha:
segs.e: So you may respond to those critics with this verse:
segs.s: several mendicants robed up in the morning and

segs.e: A liar goes to hell,
segs.s: several mendicants robed up in the morning and

segs.p: Yo vāpi katvā na karomi cāha;
segs.e: as does one who denies what they did.
segs.s: several mendicants robed up in the morning and

segs.e: Both are equal in the hereafter,
segs.s: several mendicants robed up in the morning and

segs.e: those men of base deeds.”
segs.s: several mendicants robed up in the morning and

segs.p: Atha kho te bhikkhū bhagavato santike imaṁ gāthaṁ pariyāpuṇitvā ye manussā bhikkhū disvā asabbhāhi pharusāhi vācāhi akkosanti paribhāsanti rosanti vihesanti te imāya gāthāya paṭicodenti:
segs.e: The mendicants memorized that verse in the Buddha’s presence, then used it to respond to those critics.

segs.p: Yo vāpi katvā na karomi cāha;

segs.e: People thought,

segs.p: “akārakā ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā, nayimehi kataṁ, sapantime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā”ti.
segs.e: “These ascetics who follow the Sakyan didn’t do it, it was not done by them, they swear it.”

segs.p: Neva so saddo ciraṁ ahosi. Sattāhameva ahosi. Sattāhassa accayena antaradhāyi.
segs.e: That rumor didn’t last long. It was seven days, then it vanished.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavato etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,
“It’s incredible, sir, it’s amazing!
How well said this was by the Buddha:

segs.p: ‘neso, bhikkhave, saddo ciraṁ bhavissati. Sattāhameva bhavissati. Sattāhassa accayena antaradhāyissatī’ti.
segs.e: ‘That rumor, mendicants, won’t last long. It will only be seven days, then it will vanish.’
That rumor has vanished, sir.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“People out of control stab with words,
like they stab a tusker in battle with darts.
When they hear a harsh word spoken,
a mendicant should endure with no anger in heart.”
Heartfelt Sayings 4.9
With Upasena
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmato upasenassa vaṅgantaputtassa rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: Then as Venerable Upasena son of Vaṅgantā was in private retreat this thought came to his mind:
“I’m so fortunate, so very fortunate!

segs.p: satthā ca me bhagavā arahaṁ sammāsambuddho;
segs.e: My Teacher is the Blessed One, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha.

segs.p: svākkhāte camhi dhammavinaye agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajito;
segs.e: Well explained is the teaching and training in which I have gone forth from the lay life to homelessness.
My spiritual companions are ethical and of good character.
I have fulfilled the precepts.
My mind is unified and serene.
I am a perfected one who has ended the defilements.
I am of great might and power.
My life has been good, and my death will be good.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā āyasmato upasenassa vaṅgantaputtassa cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, knowing that Venerable Upasena’s train of thought, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“One who has no guilt in life,
nor grief at facing death:
that attentive one who has seen the truth,
grieves not among the grieving.
For the mendicant with peaceful mind,
who has cut off craving for continued existence,
transmigration through births is finished,
there’ll be no more future lives for them.”
Heartfelt Sayings 4.10
The Peacefulness of Sāriputta
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā sāriputto bhagavato avidūre nisinno hoti pallaṅkaṁ ābhujitvā ujuṁ kāyaṁ paṇidhāya attano upasamaṁ paccavekkhamāno.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight, reviewing his own peacefulness.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ sāriputtaṁ avidūre nisinnaṁ pallaṅkaṁ ābhujitvā ujuṁ kāyaṁ paṇidhāya attano upasamaṁ paccavekkhamānaṁ.
segs.e: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“With mind at peace, so full of peace,
for a mendicant who has cut the cord,
transmigration through births is finished:
they’re freed from Māra’s bonds.”
Heartfelt Sayings 5.1
Who is More Dear?
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena rājā pasenadi kosalo mallikāya deviyā saddhiṁ uparipāsādavaragato hoti.
segs.e: Now at that time King Pasenadi of Kosala was upstairs in the royal longhouse together with Queen Mallikā.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo mallikaṁ deviṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi addressed Queen Mallikā,

segs.p: “atthi nu kho te, mallike, kocañño attanā piyataro”ti?
segs.e: “Mallikā, is there anyone more dear to you than yourself?”

segs.p: “Natthi kho me, mahārāja, kocañño attanā piyataro.
segs.e: “No, Great King, there isn’t.

segs.p: Tuyhaṁ pana, mahārāja, atthañño koci attanā piyataro”ti?
segs.e: But is there anyone more dear to you than yourself?”

segs.p: “Mayhampi kho, mallike, natthañño koci attanā piyataro”ti.
segs.e: “For me also, Mallikā, there’s no one.”

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo pāsādā orohitvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala came downstairs from the stilt longhouse, went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

segs.p: “Idhāhaṁ, bhante, mallikāya deviyā saddhiṁ uparipāsādavaragato mallikaṁ deviṁ etadavocaṁ:
‘atthi nu kho te, mallike, kocañño attanā piyataro’ti?
Evaṁ vutte, mallikā devī maṁ etadavoca:
‘natthi kho me, mahārāja, kocañño attanā piyataro.
Tuyhaṁ pana, mahārāja, atthañño koci attanā piyataro’ti?
Evaṁ vutte, ahaṁ, bhante, mallikaṁ deviṁ etadavocaṁ:
‘mayhampi kho, mallike, natthañño koci attanā piyataro’”ti.
Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“Having explored every quarter with the mind,
one finds no one dearer than oneself.
Likewise for others, each holds themselves dear;
so one who desires self-knowledge <j>would harm no other.”
Heartfelt Sayings 5.2
Short-lived
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā ānando sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Ānanda came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:
“It’s incredible, sir, it’s amazing!

segs.p: Yāva appāyukā hi, bhante, bhagavato mātā ahosi, sattāhajāte bhagavati bhagavato mātā kālamakāsi, tusitaṁ kāyaṁ upapajjī”ti.
segs.e: How short-lived was the Blessed One’s mother! For seven days after the Blessed One was born, his mother passed away and was reborn in the host of joyful gods.”

segs.p: “Evametaṁ, ānanda, appāyukā hi, ānanda, bodhisattamātaro honti.
segs.e: “That’s so true, Ānanda! For the mothers of beings intent of awakening are short-lived.

segs.p: Sattāhajātesu bodhisattesu bodhisattamātaro kālaṁ karonti, tusitaṁ kāyaṁ upapajjantī”ti.
segs.e: Seven days after the beings intent on awakening are born, their mothers pass away and are reborn in the host of joyful gods.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:
“Whether born or to be born,
all depart, leaving the body behind.
The skillful, understanding that all is lost,
would keenly practice the spiritual life.”
Heartfelt Sayings 5.3
With Suppabuddha the Leper
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena rājagahe suppabuddho nāma kuṭṭhī ahosi—
segs.e: At that time in Rājagaha there was a leper called Suppabuddha.
He was a poor person, destitute, and pitiful.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā mahatiyā parisāya parivuto dhammaṁ desento nisinno hoti.
segs.e: Now, at that time the Buddha was teaching Dhamma, surrounded by a large assembly.

segs.p: Addasā kho suppabuddho kuṭṭhī taṁ mahājanakāyaṁ dūratova sannipatitaṁ.
segs.e: Suppabuddha saw the crowd seated off in the distance
and thought,

segs.p: “nissaṁsayaṁ kho ettha kiñci khādanīyaṁ vā bhojanīyaṁ vā bhājīyati.
segs.e: “Surely some fresh and cooked foods will be distributed there.
Why don’t I approach the crowd?

segs.p: Appeva nāmettha kiñci khādanīyaṁ vā bhojanīyaṁ vā labheyyan”ti.
segs.e: Hopefully I’ll get something to eat.”

segs.p: Atha kho suppabuddho kuṭṭhī yena so mahājanakāyo tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: So he approached the crowd

segs.p: Addasā kho suppabuddho kuṭṭhī bhagavantaṁ mahatiyā parisāya parivutaṁ dhammaṁ desentaṁ nisinnaṁ.
segs.e: where he saw the Buddha teaching Dhamma, surrounded by a large assembly.
When he saw this he thought,

segs.p: “na kho ettha kiñci khādanīyaṁ vā bhojanīyaṁ vā bhājīyati.
segs.e: “There’s no food being distributed here.

segs.p: Samaṇo ayaṁ gotamo parisati dhammaṁ deseti.
segs.e: The ascetic Gotama is teaching Dhamma in an assembly.
Why don’t I also listen to the teaching?”
Right there he sat down to one side, thinking,
“I also will listen to the teaching.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā sabbāvantaṁ parisaṁ cetasā ceto paricca manasākāsi
segs.e: Then the Buddha focused on encompassing the minds of everyone in the assembly, thinking,

segs.p: “ko nu kho idha bhabbo dhammaṁ viññātun”ti?
segs.e: “Who here is capable of understanding the teaching?”

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā suppabuddhaṁ kuṭṭhiṁ tassaṁ parisāyaṁ nisinnaṁ.
segs.e: He saw Suppabuddha sitting in the assembly,
and thought,
“He is capable of understanding the teaching.”

segs.p: Suppabuddhaṁ kuṭṭhiṁ ārabbha anupubbiṁ kathaṁ kathesi, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: He gave a step by step talk especially for Suppabuddha

segs.p: dānakathaṁ sīlakathaṁ saggakathaṁ; kāmānaṁ ādīnavaṁ okāraṁ saṅkilesaṁ; nekkhamme ānisaṁsaṁ pakāsesi.
segs.e: on giving, ethical conduct, and heaven. He revealed the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, so sordid and corrupt, and the benefit of renunciation.

segs.p: Yadā bhagavā aññāsi suppabuddhaṁ kuṭṭhiṁ kallacittaṁ muducittaṁ vinīvaraṇacittaṁ udaggacittaṁ pasannacittaṁ, atha yā buddhānaṁ sāmukkaṁsikā dhammadesanā taṁ pakāsesi—
segs.e: When the Buddha knew that Suppabuddha’s mind was ready, pliable, rid of hindrances, elated, and confident he revealed the special teaching of the Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi nāma suddhaṁ vatthaṁ apagatakāḷakaṁ sammadeva rajanaṁ paṭiggaṇheyya;
segs.e: Just as a clean cloth rid of stains would properly absorb dye,

segs.p: evamevaṁ suppabuddhassa kuṭṭhissa tasmiṁyeva āsane virajaṁ vītamalaṁ dhammacakkhuṁ udapādi:
segs.e: in that very seat the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in Suppabuddha:
“Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.”

segs.p: Atha kho suppabuddho kuṭṭhī diṭṭhadhammo pattadhammo viditadhammo pariyogāḷhadhammo tiṇṇavicikiccho vigatakathaṅkatho vesārajjappatto aparappaccayo satthu sāsane uṭṭhāyāsanā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho suppabuddho kuṭṭhī bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Suppabuddha saw, attained, understood, and fathomed the Dhamma. He went beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, and became self-assured and independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instructions. He rose from his seat and went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said:
“Excellent, sir! Excellent!

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhante, nikkujjitaṁ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṁ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṁ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṁ dhāreyya: ‘cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī’ti; evamevaṁ bhagavatā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito.
segs.e: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

segs.p: Esāhaṁ, bhante, bhagavantaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca.
segs.e: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

segs.p: Upāsakaṁ maṁ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṁ saraṇaṁ gatan”ti.
segs.e: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

segs.p: Atha kho suppabuddho kuṭṭhī bhagavatā dhammiyā kathāya sandassito samādapito samuttejito sampahaṁsito bhagavatā bhāsitaṁ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā pakkāmi.
